query: Which HTML5 semantic tag should be used to wrap a blog post or independent product card that can be syndicated?
reference: The <article> tag represents a self-contained composition that is independently distributable, such as a blog post or product card.

query: In flexbox, how does align-items behave by default when no value is provided on the flex container?
reference: By default, align-items defaults to stretch, which stretches flex items to fill the container along the cross axis.

query: What is the specific purpose of the <footer> semantic tag according to HTML5 standards?
reference: The <footer> tag contains author information, copyright data, or footer links.

query: If I set flex: 1 1 auto; on a flex item, what do the three individual values represent?
reference: In the flex shorthand, the three values correspond to flex-grow (1), flex-shrink (1), and flex-basis (auto).

query: Why would screen readers (A11y) struggle if an entire website is built using only <div> tags instead of semantic tags?
reference: Semantic HTML clearly describes meaning to assistive tech and screen-readers; generic divs lack semantic landmarks like main, nav, and header.

query: How do you define a 3-column equal-width responsive grid using the fractional unit (fr) in CSS Grid?
reference: Use grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); on a display: grid container.

query: What is the difference between space-between and space-evenly in flexbox justify-content?
reference: space-between puts equal space between items with first/last flush to edges; space-evenly distributes equal space between and around all items.

query: Explain how the flex-direction property influences the orientation of the main axis and cross axis.
reference: flex-direction determines the main axis (row is horizontal, column is vertical); the cross axis runs perpendicular to the main axis.

query: In CSS box model, is the transparent space outside the element border referred to as margin or padding?
reference: Margin is the transparent space outside the border that separates the element from neighboring elements.

query: Can an individual flex item override its container's align-items setting, and which property does it use?
reference: Yes, an individual flex child can override container cross-axis alignment using the align-self property.

query: How does CSS Grid span an element across two columns from grid line 1 to grid line 3?
reference: Use grid-column: 1 / 3; to span from vertical grid line 1 to grid line 3.

query: What is the role of <nav> in an HTML document and can multiple nav blocks exist on a page?
reference: The <nav> tag defines a set of major navigation links; multiple nav elements can exist for header navigation, pagination, or footers.

query: Under content-box, if width is 200px, padding is 20px, and border is 5px, what is the total rendered width?
reference: Total rendered width is 200 + 20(left) + 20(right) + 5(left) + 5(right) = 250px.

query: Explain the difference between 1-dimensional and 2-dimensional layouts in modern CSS design.
reference: Flexbox is 1-dimensional (arranging items in a single row or column), whereas CSS Grid is 2-dimensional (handling rows and columns simultaneously).

query: Why is gap preferred over child margins when spacing items inside flex and grid containers?
reference: The gap property applies clean spacing strictly between adjacent items without adding unwanted outer margins to the perimeter.

query: yo how do i make flex items wrap into multiple rows when they run out of screen space??
reference: Set flex-wrap: wrap; on the flex container to allow items to break into new rows.

query: what does the <section> element designate compared to a generic container?
reference: <section> represents a standalone section of functionality or thematic grouping of content.

query: Explain flex-shrink: 0; behavior during container viewport narrowing.
reference: flex-shrink: 0 prevents the item from shrinking smaller than its flex-basis or content width when the container narrows.

query: Does the <header> element only apply to the top of the entire webpage or can it belong to an <article>?
reference: <header> represents introductory content; it can be used for the page header or as an intro header inside an <article> or <section>.

query: What happens when flex-direction is set to column-reverse in terms of child visual layout and main axis orientation?
reference: column-reverse sets the main axis vertically with items stacked from bottom to top in reverse order.

query: In CSS Grid, how does grid-template-rows define horizontal row track sizes?
reference: grid-template-rows defines the line names and track sizing functions of the grid rows.

query: Which box model layer sits immediately between the element content and the border?
reference: Padding sits directly between the content and the border, clearing space around the content inside the border.

query: Why does * { box-sizing: border-box; } simplify responsive grid and percentage-based width calculations?
reference: Because padding and border are included within the declared percentage width, preventing unexpected line breaks and overflow.

query: can grid-row: 2 / 4; be used to span multiple horizontal tracks in css grid?
reference: Yes, grid-row: 2 / 4 spans from horizontal grid line 2 to line 4 across two row tracks.

query: When creating a site layout, when should a developer choose CSS Grid over Flexbox?
reference: CSS Grid is preferred for full-page, 2-dimensional layouts (rows and columns together), while Flexbox is preferred for 1-dimensional component alignment.

query: What happens if a developer attempts to access a variable declared with let before its declaration line?
reference: Accessing a let variable before its declaration throws a ReferenceError because it resides in the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ).

query: Do arrow functions have their own arguments object, and if not, what ES6 feature replaces it?
reference: No, arrow functions do not have an arguments object; rest parameters (...args) are used instead.

query: Explain why invoking an arrow function with the new operator throws a TypeError.
reference: Arrow functions lack a [[Construct]] method and prototype property, so invoking them with new throws a TypeError.

query: How does Object.freeze() affect nested objects inside a frozen JavaScript object?
reference: Object.freeze() is shallow; properties referencing nested objects remain mutable unless recursively frozen.

query: In the JavaScript event loop, which queue takes precedence when the call stack clears: microtasks or macrotasks?
reference: The microtask queue (Promises) has higher priority and empties immediately after the call stack clears before any macrotask runs.

query: Show how to provide a default value when destructuring a property from an object in ES6.
reference: Use const { name, role = 'student' } = user; to specify a default fallback value.

query: Does the spread operator ({ ...obj }) perform a deep clone or a shallow clone of an object?
reference: The spread operator performs a shallow copy; nested object references are copied rather than duplicated.

query: What are the three possible states of a JavaScript Promise?
reference: A Promise exists in one of three states: Pending, Fulfilled, or Rejected.

query: Why can properties of an array declared with const still be pushed to or modified without error?
reference: const prevents variable identifier reassignment, but the underlying object or array in memory remains mutable.

query: How do rest parameters gather an indefinite number of function arguments into an array in ES6?
reference: Prefixing the last parameter with three dots (...args) captures remaining arguments into a true JavaScript array.

query: What is the key scoping difference between var and let in JavaScript?
reference: var is function-scoped (or global), whereas let is block-scoped (confined strictly within curly braces {}).

query: Why did ES6 arrow functions eliminate the need for patterns like const self = this or .bind(this)?
reference: Arrow functions inherit lexical this from their enclosing execution scope, avoiding manual this rebinding.

query: How should errors be caught when handling asynchronous operations using async and await?
reference: Wrap the awaited asynchronous expressions inside a synchronous-style try/catch block.

query: does setTimeout callback execute in the microtask queue or the macrotask/task queue?
reference: setTimeout callbacks are queued in the macrotask (Task/Callback) queue, not the microtask queue.

query: Can a variable declared with var be re-declared in the exact same scope without throwing an error?
reference: Yes, var permits re-declaration within the same scope, which often created subtle bugs in legacy JavaScript.

query: What syntax extracts the first and second elements of an array and groups the remainder into a variable?
reference: Use array destructuring with rest: const [first, second, ...remaining] = items;.

query: What happens if a developer reassigns a variable declared with const?
reference: Reassigning a const identifier throws a TypeError at runtime because const bindings are immutable.

query: Explain what queueMicrotask() does in modern JavaScript execution.
reference: queueMicrotask queues a callback on the microtask queue, which executes immediately after current synchronous execution clears.

query: yo if i do const obj = Object.freeze({ a: 1 }); can i add obj.b = 2??
reference: No, Object.freeze prevents adding new properties, deleting existing ones, or modifying values.

query: How is a Promise created using its constructor and what two callback parameters are passed to the executor?
reference: A Promise is constructed via new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... }).

query: What are the two golden rules of React Hooks regarding where they can be called?
reference: 1. Only call hooks at top level (never inside loops, conditions, or nested functions), 2. Only call hooks from React function components or custom hooks.

query: Why should you use the functional update form setCount(prev => prev + 1) in useState?
reference: The functional update receives the latest pending state, preventing stale state bugs when updates are batched.

query: How do you run a useEffect hook strictly once when the component mounts and cleanup on unmount?
reference: Pass an empty dependency array [] to useEffect to execute strictly on mount and cleanup on unmount.

query: Does mutating the .current property of a useRef hook cause a component re-render?
reference: No, mutating .current persists values across renders without triggering a component re-render.

query: What is the primary problem that useContext solves in deeply nested component trees?
reference: useContext eliminates prop drilling by allowing child components anywhere in the tree to access shared state directly.

query: What is the difference between useMemo and useCallback in React?
reference: useMemo memoizes the computed result of a function, whereas useCallback memoizes the callback function instance itself.

query: How does returning a cleanup function from useEffect prevent memory leaks in web applications?
reference: The cleanup function cancels active timers, unsubscribes from event emitters, and aborts pending network requests when components unmount.

query: Give a common use case for useRef that interacts directly with browser DOM elements.
reference: Focusing a text input directly via inputRef.current.focus() or measuring DOM dimensions.

query: What happens if a useEffect hook has no dependency array passed to it?
reference: If omitted, the effect callback executes after every single render of the component.

query: How do you provide a value to all child consumers using a context created with createContext?
reference: Wrap consuming components in <MyContext.Provider value={{ ... }}>{children}</MyContext.Provider>.

query: Why does passing an unmemoized callback to a child wrapped in React.memo defeat child memoization?
reference: A new function reference is created on every parent render, causing shallow prop comparison in React.memo to fail.

query: Can a custom hook call built-in React hooks like useState and useEffect internally?
reference: Yes, custom hooks are JavaScript functions whose names start with 'use' that can call built-in hooks to share stateful logic.

query: How do you store a setInterval timer ID across renders without causing infinite re-renders?
reference: Store the timer ID in a ref (timerRef.current = setInterval(...)) because modifying a ref does not trigger a re-render.

query: how do i consume auth context in a functional header component??
reference: Call const { user, logout } = useContext(AuthContext); inside the functional component.

query: When does React run the cleanup function of a useEffect that has [count] in its dependency array?
reference: It runs the cleanup before re-running the effect with the new value, as well as upon final component unmount.

query: How does Node.js handle blocking asynchronous I/O despite having a single main execution thread?
reference: Node.js offloads blocking I/O (filesystem, DNS, crypto) to the libuv background thread pool while the event loop stays responsive.

query: What are the exact four parameters required in order to define an error-handling middleware in Express?
reference: Error-handling middleware functions require exactly four arguments: (err, req, res, next).

query: Which HTTP status code signifies that a request lacks a valid JSON Web Token for authentication?
reference: HTTP 401 Unauthorized indicates that the request lacks a valid authentication token.

query: What are the three dot-separated components of a JSON Web Token (JWT)?
reference: A JWT consists of Header.Payload.Signature encoded in Base64Url format.

query: Why should CPU-intensive operations like high-iteration password hashing not be executed on Node's main thread?
reference: CPU-intensive tasks block the single JavaScript execution thread, preventing the event loop from handling incoming network requests.

query: What built-in Express middleware parses incoming requests with JSON payloads?
reference: Use app.use(express.json()); which parses incoming request bodies with JSON payloads.

query: What is the difference between HTTP 401 Unauthorized and HTTP 403 Forbidden in RESTful APIs?
reference: 401 means the client is unauthenticated (missing/invalid token); 403 means the user is authenticated but lacks required authorization permissions.

query: What HTTP method should be used for partially modifying specific fields of an existing user resource in REST design?
reference: PATCH is used to partially update specific fields, whereas PUT completely replaces the resource.

query: How does middleware pass execution flow to the subsequent middleware function in the Express pipeline?
reference: Middleware calls next() to pass execution flow to the next handler in the stack.

query: In standard REST URL design, why are plural nouns like /api/students preferred over verbs like /api/getStudents?
reference: REST URLs are resource-oriented using plural nouns; actions are communicated via standard HTTP verbs (GET, POST, etc.).

query: In JWT authentication, where does the client typically send the token on protected HTTP requests?
reference: Clients send the token in the Authorization request header formatted as Bearer <token>.

query: Which event loop phase executes callbacks scheduled with setImmediate() in Node.js?
reference: setImmediate() callbacks run in the Check phase of the Node.js event loop.

query: What HTTP status code should be returned after successfully creating a new course via a POST endpoint?
reference: Return HTTP 201 Created to indicate the resource was successfully created.

query: yo how do i sign a token with 7 days expiration in jsonwebtoken library??
reference: Call jwt.sign({ id: user.id, role: 'STUDENT' }, SECRET, { expiresIn: '7d' });.

query: What happens if a middleware function neither sends a response nor calls next()?
reference: The request-response cycle will hang indefinitely until the client or server times out.

query: What are the specific requirements for a database relation to satisfy First Normal Form (1NF)?
reference: 1NF requires atomic (indivisible) column values, unique rows, and an identified primary key.

query: How is a Many-to-Many relationship modeled in relational database design?
reference: Using a junction (bridge) table containing foreign keys referencing both parent tables, often combined into a composite primary key.

query: What constitutes a transitive dependency in Second Normal Form, and how does 3NF eliminate it?
reference: A transitive dependency occurs when a non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute; 3NF eliminates it by moving them into a separate table.

query: What search time complexity does a PostgreSQL B-tree index provide for equality lookups?
reference: A B-tree index provides logarithmic O(log N) lookups for equality and range queries.

query: Explain what the Durability property in ACID transactions guarantees in the event of a server power failure.
reference: Durability guarantees committed changes are permanently recorded in non-volatile storage (WAL) and survive system crashes or power failures.

query: What are two performance trade-offs or penalties of adding excessive B-tree indexes to a table?
reference: Indexes consume additional disk storage and add write latency to INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE queries because index trees must be updated.

query: Why does a database query planner choose a Sequential Scan (Seq Scan) over an Index Scan on small tables?
reference: Reading a few contiguous disk pages sequentially is faster than traversing index tree branches and fetching random heap pages.

query: What is the Leftmost Prefix Rule in PostgreSQL composite indexes on columns (A, B)?
reference: Queries filtering by column A (or A and B) can utilize the index, but queries filtering solely by column B cannot.

query: What is a Foreign Key and what database guarantee does it enforce between two tables?
reference: A foreign key points to a primary key in another table, enforcing referential integrity by preventing orphan records.

query: What SQL commands start a new transaction block and safely cancel all modifications on failure?
reference: Use BEGIN; to start a transaction block and ROLLBACK; to discard all modifications.

query: Explain the Atomicity property in ACID transactions using a student bank transfer example.
reference: Atomicity ensures all statements succeed or none do; if debit succeeds but credit fails, the entire transaction rolls back.

query: What is Second Normal Form (2NF) and what kind of dependency does it explicitly ban on composite keys?
reference: 2NF requires 1NF and mandates that no non-key attribute is partially dependent on only part of a composite primary key.

query: What concurrency phenomena does the Isolation property in ACID transactions aim to prevent?
reference: Isolation prevents concurrent transactions from interfering, avoiding dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads.

query: Can a primary key column contain NULL values in a relational PostgreSQL table?
reference: No, primary key values must be unique and cannot contain NULL.

query: yo how do i index a column so range queries like score >= 80 run fast in postgres??
reference: Create a default B-tree index: CREATE INDEX idx_scores ON students(score); which optimizes equality and range queries.

query: How should responsive CSS Flexbox classes be integrated with conditional React JSX rendering without breaking layout flow?
reference: Apply display: flex and flex properties to parent wrapper divs/elements while conditionally rendering child items.

query: How does an Axios or fetch call from a React component authenticate against a protected Express JWT endpoint?
reference: The React client retrieves the token (from context or state) and includes it in the HTTP Authorization header as Bearer <token>.

query: How does an Express request handler ensure a multi-step financial transaction respects ACID Atomicity in PostgreSQL?
reference: The Express controller executes queries within BEGIN and COMMIT blocks, executing ROLLBACK inside a catch block if any error occurs.

query: Compare the execution priority of a JavaScript Promise microtask with an Express setImmediate callback in Node.js.
reference: Promise microtasks run immediately after the current JavaScript call stack clears, before the event loop advances to the setImmediate Check phase.

query: Explain how database normalization (3NF) in PostgreSQL affects the shape of JSON state managed by useState in React.
reference: Normalized tables return relational rows requiring joins or foreign key references, encouraging normalized or nested object state in React components.

query: Why does mutating a JavaScript object property directly violate both const immutability principles and React state re-rendering?
reference: React compares state references by identity (Object.is); in-place mutation does not create a new object reference, so React fails to trigger a re-render.

query: When building an HTML table to display students and enrolled courses, how does a SQL Many-to-Many junction table supply the data?
reference: A SQL query joins students, junction table, and courses, producing tabular rows that populate HTML <tr> and <td> table structures.

query: Trace a full-stack flow: a student clicks Delete Account in React, Express verifies JWT and authorization, and PostgreSQL executes a transaction.
reference: React issues authenticated DELETE request with Bearer token; Express validates JWT role, then runs SQL transaction to remove user and foreign key references.

query: When an Express endpoint returns an HTTP 401 response, how does a React application update its authentication context?
reference: The React fetch handler catches the 401 status, triggers the AuthContext logout updater, and clears the user state and token.

query: How does an Express static middleware server serve semantic HTML5 pages and CSS stylesheets to client browsers?
reference: app.use(express.static('public')) serves static HTML and CSS asset files directly to requesting HTTP clients.
